title: Maryland’s moment: Protecting Marylanders from high drug costs
summary: Maryland is showing what's possible at the state level to rein in drug costs, writes David Conway, but it can't let up now, as a growing senior population and higher need make efforts like the Prescription Drug Affordability Board all the more important.
content:
by David Conway, Maryland Matters March 17, 2026

by David Conway, Maryland Matters March 17, 2026

Each morning, thousands of older Marylanders deal with the daily challenges of managing chronic health conditions. For many, staying healthy depends on reliable access to prescription drugs. But as drug prices continue to rise, older adults are forced to make impossible choices: between groceries and diabetes drugs, between keeping the lights on and accessing their medications.

As president of AARP Maryland, I hear these stories every day. It goes without saying that many people in our state are struggling to keep up with rising costs. This is even  more difficult for older adults. In Maryland,  57% of Medicare beneficiaries report having multiple chronic conditions. For them, skipping a dose isn’t just risky; it can be life-threatening. When access to medication becomes uncertain, the impacts can be severe, leading to further health complications, repeated emergency hospital visits, or even mortality.

Prescription drug costs have soared, outpacing wages and straining family budgets. Nationally, one in four Americans reports difficulty affording their medications. Marylanders are no exception. For older adults on fixed incomes, even small price increases can mean going without. These aren’t abstract numbers – they represent real people forced to choose between their health and their basic needs.

Our state has both the power and the responsibility to protect its aging population, and right now Maryland’s leaders are showing what’s possible. These state-level solutions are especially critical for seniors, who are often most affected by gaps in federal policy.

Consider the story of Larry Zarzecki, a Marylander and retired police officer, who lost his home and retirement savings in attempts to afford his Parkinson’s disease medication. His situation was the unfortunate consequence of inaction from the federal government, leading to drug companies continuing to unconscionably raise prices. Although Mr. Zarzecki now benefits from the prescription drug negotiation provisions of the landmark Inflation Reduction Act, Marylanders under 65 are left struggling to afford the medicines they need.

Maryland isn’t waiting for Washington to fix this. In 2019, our state created its Prescription Drug Affordability Board (PDAB), an innovative model that puts the power back in the hands of state leaders. These boards are uniquely empowered to review prescription drug costs and, in some cases, set “upper payment limits” (UPLs) on what government entities pay.

Our state’s leaders recognized early that they could not wait for federal solutions. Maryland’s PDAB has identified high-cost drugs, such as Jardiance and Farxiga, that are straining public budgets and household finances alike. Anti-diabetic drugs, such as these, are one of the largest expenditures of Maryland state government health plans.

As a next step, the board is preparing to set UPLs for these drugs, initially covering state and local government purchases. This is a huge step in the right direction for protecting older Marylanders, and there’s more to come. Once UPLs are implemented for state and local governments, the law allows for expansion to all Marylanders after a year. For patients, this means greater protection against skyrocketing drug prices and a better chance of accessing necessary medications without financial hardship. This means Maryland is setting the stage for a future where life-saving medications are priced fairly, not just for government programs, but for every resident in the state.

The potential impact is enormous. If UPLs are set and expanded, thousands of seniors could see prescription costs drop, putting money back in the pockets of people who need it most. Lower out-of-pocket costs mean more Marylanders can stick to their treatment plans, avoid costly hospital stays and live healthier, more independent lives.

Our PDAB has paved the way, but now, urgency is critical. High drug costs continue to burden families and limit access to life-saving treatments. Without broad and fast implementation, too many Marylanders remain vulnerable.

I appreciate the board moving quickly to implement UPLs for medications like Jardiance and Farxiga. The sooner this happens for state and local government, the sooner all Marylanders, especially seniors, can benefit.

As our population ages, Maryland’s responsibility to act only grows. By 2030, a quarter of our residents will be over 60, and the prevalence of chronic diseases will rise. We cannot allow high drug costs to keep anyone from the medicines they need to stay healthy and independent.

Thank you to our state leaders, the PDAB and advocates who have worked so hard to get us here. I look forward to a future where no Maryland senior is left behind, and soon, the nation will see what’s possible when states lead the way.
